title: Compositional Symbolic Execution à la Carte (Extended Version)
comment: Extended version, with appendices, of the corresponding POPL'27 paper
summary: We introduce compositional symbolic execution à la carte, a modular approach for building compositional symbolic execution (CSE) tools, powered by combinator-based design of key components, including memory models, management and automation of user-defined predicates, and bi-abductive analysis. Our approach is grounded on meta-theory mechanised in the Rocq proof assistant and allows tool developers to easily build correct-by-construction CSE tools for symbolic analysis of their programming languages of choice, with minimal implementation and proof effort. We show how our approach scales to real-world languages by implementing it in Gillian, a state-of-the-art CSE tool, and using it to capture the intricacies of the memory models of C, JavaScript, and Rust. We evaluate our approach by running all of the relevant previous case studies of Gillian, showing no unexpected behaviours and comparable performance.

title: Denotational Results in Compiler Correctness and Comparisons with Operational Approaches
summary:
Anyone setting out to prove a compiler correct must choose a style of semantics. The CakeML and CompCert projects, among others, show that operational semantics such as abstract machines and interpreters are viable choices. In this paper we explore whether denotational semantics can also be used in proofs of compiler correctness and evaluate the tradeoffs. We focus on a compiler from FPC, a language with lexically scoped functions and recursive types, to a first-order low-level intermediate language. This compiler includes closure conversion, but no prior proof of correctness with respect to denotational semantics covers closure conversion for a Turing-complete language. Compiler correctness requires that the denotation of a program be both preserved and reflected by the compiler. For closure conversion, reflection is the hard direction. We present the first denotational proofs of semantic reflection for closure conversion applied to a Turing-complete language, one proof with respect to a graph model and one with respect to Scott domains. For the graph-model proof we develop a new logical relation, the approximant logical relation, and for the Scott-domain proof we adapt a logical relation of Reynolds.
  As a first step in evaluating the tradeoffs, we compare mechanized correctness proofs of an eight-pass compiler, from FPC down to a typed low-level intermediate language, in five semantic styles. Two of the styles are denotational and three are operational. We find that no one semantics yields the shortest proofs for every compiler pass. We identify two factors that influence proof size. For operational semantics, proof size tends to grow with how much the runs of the source and target differ. For denotational semantics, the proofs are succinct when the correctness of a pass is an equation between meanings, and lengthy when a pass needs a logical relation.

title: Defining the mathematical family tree with a minimal programming language
comment: 33 pages. https://tegmark.org/mathtree includes and interactive MLISP calculator and a detailed atlas of the mathematical theories and structures
summary:
I introduce MLISP, a Turing-complete language with nine single-character commands (a b c d f 0 i j k), and use it to define 88 mathematical structures and a family tree of 65 theories that they model, with three aims:
  Pedagogy: It presents the mathematical structures in a unified way, with standardized presentation tableaus that define them and axiomatized theories that describe them.
  Connections: It highlights how they are related in the family tree via added symbols, axioms, etc. While the full tree is obviously infinite, its lower parts naturally separate into six main branches: the relational branch, the algebraic branch, the logic branch, the number branch, the set branch and the continuum branch.
  Foundations: The definitions, key theorems and models of each entry are verified in Lean. Mathematical structures are defined as equivalence classes of presentations, which in a constructivist spirit are defined in a simple, explicit and self-contained way in standardized presentation tableaus with minimal human baggage. For finite structures, the generating functions are defined by lookup tables. For countably infinite ones, they are instead defined computationally using MLISP, since more complex languages such as Lean are massive overkill for rigorously defining standard arithmetic operations (for example, the program "jibjbfid" defines subtraction).
  An interactive version is available at https://tegmark.org/mathtree. The Lean code is public, also verifies the correctness of MLISP and includes 43% of the theorems from Mathlib 2026-10-11. \end{abstract}

title: A Calculus for Borrowability
summary: Borrowing grants temporary shared or exclusive access to a linear resource without transferring ownership. However, capturing borrowing in a type system poses two challenges: a lender, the reference a borrow was taken from, should remain a first-class value that can be moved, and regain its permission when a non-lexical borrow ends. We propose borrowability, an index on reference types that tracks how access permissions are lent across lifetimes while separating them from the owner's obligation to release the resource. A lender is then an ordinary value whose borrowability records its remaining access permissions and the lifetimes of its active borrows, recovering borrowed permissions in place when those lifetimes end. We formalize borrowability in the calculus $λ^{boρ}$, mechanize its semantic type soundness and memory safety proofs in Rocq using Iris, and show that our design rules out all 24 in-scope soundness issues reported against the Rust compiler.

title: Functional Programming with Hypergraph Transformation
summary:
Complex data structures are difficult to manipulate declaratively while preserving their shape invariants. Functional languages offer pattern matching and strong static guarantees, but their type systems primarily describe tree-shaped data. Graph transformation languages support richer structures, yet their state-oriented models do not integrate naturally with value- and function-based programming.
  This dissertation introduces $λ_{GT}$, a functional language that integrates port-hypergraph transformation. It represents complex data as port hypergraphs, manipulates them by pattern matching, and uses types to specify global shape invariants. We formalise HyperLMNtal as a term-based graph transformation formalism, then define the syntax and call-by-value semantics of untyped $λ_{GT}$ and implement a prototype interpreter.
  We develop a core type system for $λ_{GT}$, prove its soundness, and relate it to graph-grammar-based typing. We extend the system with linear implication types to describe incomplete graphs arising during pattern matching. The extended system is sound with dynamic pattern-matching checks and is conservative over complete graph types. We also identify a statically safe fragment in which these checks can be eliminated. Finally, we mechanise the definitions and meta-theory in Isabelle/HOL.

title: Verifying Type Soundness for Nontransitive Information Flow Security
summary: We present a machine-checked soundness proof of a type system for the nontransitive noninterference (NTNI) information flow security property in an imperative programming language using Dafny. The original formulation of NTNI was developed for a functional programming language augmented with memory access operators, where security policies are expressed as coarse-grained information flow constraints over component-based software systems. Although subsequent research has extended NTNI type systems in various directions, to the best of our knowledge, no prior work has established a machine-checked soundness proof for type-enforced NTNI. As a result, the correctness of existing NTNI enforcement mechanisms has not been formally verified with a high degree of assurance.

title: Vx: A Programming Language for Scalable, Maintainable and Secure Systems
summary: A program for a modern machine runs on several kinds of chips. Its memory spaces, links and capacities are invisible to the compilers of today. So a host that reads device memory, a working set that does not fit, or a data race shows up only when the program runs. Vx is a systems programming language that puts these facts in the program text. A machine is a source file of declarations. A value's type says which memory it lives in. Apart from one stated exception, a function's signature is the whole contract that its callers see. A flag lists the code and the facts that the compiler trusts without a proof. This report is a tour of the language at one commit. It describes six design principles, the core language, and the features that serve three qualities. Vx is scalable because one program text runs across machines, cores and GPU threads. With an option, the compiler also checks its function bodies in parallel. It is maintainable because a signature is the contract of a function and most diagnostics have codes. The output of the parallel compiler does not depend on the number of threads. It is secure because safe code has ownership, borrow, race and placement checks, and in safe code, a file or a socket of the standard library opens only with a right. For every feature, the report gives its status and the evidence for it. It also lists where the implementation does not yet meet the design.

title: Increasing the Precision of IR Mapping for Incremental Data Analysis
summary: Static analysis tools operate on an Intermediate Representation (IR) --- an internal model of the program on which dataflow analysis computes and stores facts against IR object identifiers. Incremental dataflow analysis reuses these cached facts across consecutive program versions, but requires an accurate mapping between IR objects in the old and new versions. When this mapping is imprecise, the consequence is not merely a missed optimization: unmapped IR objects inflate the change set, increasing the number of program points that the analyzer must recompute and forcing it to redo work that a more precise mapping would have avoided. This cost is not specific to any one kind of IR object; it arises wherever IR-level identity is unstable across versions. Any IR that decomposes nested source expressions generates temporary variables which are assigned names by a method-local counter that shifts whenever a statement is inserted or deleted earlier in the method, breaking any name- or attribute-based mapping. We present a systematic algorithm that establishes a sound, oneto-one mapping of these temporary variables across consecutive versions, and formalize and prove the soundness of the mapping, guaranteeing that every produced mapping is semantically correct. The resulting precise mapping shrinks the change set, reducing the number of program points the incremental analysis must recompute. Implemented within the Soot framework for Jimple IR and evaluated on 8 real-world Java projects with genuine edits from the BUGSWARM dataset, our approach reduces the IR change set by over 82% on average compared to Reviser's graph-differencing algorithm, while completing the full pipeline within 250 ms per project---directly countering the common assumption that a more precise change set necessarily costs more time to compute.
